newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan may not see foreign telecom investment flood. [CORRECTED 09:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Japan may not see foreign telecom investment flood. [CORRECTED 09:45 GMT]

text.p: A sweeping pact to open up the world"s vast telecoms market could bring cheaper international services to Japan, but analysts questioned whether it would prompt floods of foreign investment in Japan.
Sixty-eight countries agreed on Saturday to the pact to open the world"s $600 billion telecommunications market to competition, clinching the deal just hours before a midnight deadline.
Japanese Posts and Telecommunications Minister Hisao Horinouchi welcomed the agreement, which he said would help cut costs and bring a wider range of services to customers.

"The success of the negotiations in introducing liberalisation and competition to the field of telecommunications will enable rates to be reduced and services to be diversified," Horinouchi said in a statement on Sunday.

Japan, whose 15.6 percent share of global revenues makes it the world"s third largest telecom market, agreed under the deal to remove its 33 percent ceiling on foreign investment in most carriers and radio-based services.
But Tokyo resisted U.S. pressure to remove its 20 percent ceiling on foreign stakes in giant NTT (Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp ) and KDD (Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd).

"Some say that Japan"s restrictions on KDD and NTT are a problem, but we think the U.S. limit of 20 percent on foreign investment in operators with radio licences is the problem," a Posts and Telecommunications official told Reuters.

"If the United States, the European Union and Canada were willing to improve their positions (on foreign investment), then Japan would be willing to discuss it," he said, adding Tokyo did not intend to enter two-way talks with Washington.
Some industry analysts said the deal would likely lower international telecom costs for Japanese customers.

"International telecom service has been a kind of cartel and rates have been kept artificially high," said Toshiaki Iba, an analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Asia. "Now that cartel structure will unravel and rates will come down."
Others were not so sure.
"It is generally said that if foreign carriers come in, charges would come down, but I don"t see any logical connection," said Kiyohisa Ota, a Merrill Lynch Japan analyst.

Japan had already indicated its willingness to remove its 33 percent ceiling on foreign stakes in carriers other than KDD and NTT, a move analysts said fit into a broader effort to allow more competition to cut costs and rejuvenate industry.
"Basically, they want to make the telecom industry in Japan more and more competitive, not only domestically but on a global scale," said Eric Gan, analyst at Goldman Sachs (Japan).
"That"s why they are lifting a lot of restrictions...and looking at other areas to introduce competition, bring down prices and make the industry more competitive," he said.

Analysts said an injection of foreign capital would be a good thing for the industry. But some questioned whether many foreign firms would be keen to spend the big sums needed to take controlling stakes in firms like NTT"s long-distance rivals, Japan Telecom Co Ltd and DDI Corp.

"There aren"t so many foreign companies with that much money, and I don"t think Japan Telecom and DDI are that attractive. They are too expensive at their current share prices," said Dresdner Kleinwort's (corrects from "Goldman Sach's") Iba. "And I don"t think Japan Telecom or DDI would want to come under foreign control."
Washington is likely to keep pressing Tokyo to remove its limits on foreign investment in NTT and KDD, and NTT for one said it expected the government to do so eventually.
"In future there will probably be a trend in countries including Japan to remove such restrictions, and we expect them ultimately to be removed," an NTT spokesman told Reuters.

Foreign carriers such as British Telecommunications Plc are keen to cozy up to NTT to beef up their global alliances, especially now that NTT has won the right to offer international services as part of a major restructuring.
"Everyone wants to tie up with NTT to set up their global franchise," Gan said, adding some foreign firms might want at least a one-third stake in order to gain a say in management.

Still, many analysts say any BT-NTT link would at first stop short of cross-shareholding, while some said that grabbing more than 20 percent of NTT would be tough since the government still owns about two-thirds of the former state-owned monopoly.
So why the fuss from Washington? "It"s a matter of principle," Iba said.
